name: Guevarism
summary: Guevarism is the revolutionary Marxism-Leninism associated with Che Guevara: armed insurrection by a small guerrilla vanguard (the foco) can create the conditions for revolution, especially in the rural periphery. It couples this with proletarian internationalism, hard anti-imperialism, state-led socialist construction, and moral rather than material incentives to forge a selfless 'New Man'.
scope: Guevarism as its defining sources describe it (Cancino, s6; Löwy, s7): the revolutionary Marxism-Leninism of Che Guevara (c. 1959-1967), a current of the 1960s new left built on the foco doctrine, proletarian internationalism, central planning with moral incentives and the new man. Its texts are Guevara's own: the key texts Cancino names (Notes for the Study of the Ideology of the Cuban Revolution, Socialism and Man in Cuba, the Message to the Tricontinental) and his other speeches and essays (Algiers, Guerrilla warfare: A method, the budgetary finance system). Later guerrilla movements in the guevarist tradition (the Zapatistas, the Tupamaros) and Régis Debray's systematisation are other subjects. Guevarism was never a state's official doctrine, so it has no record of its own: Cuba's government practice is Fidelismo's and Cuban Marxism-Leninism's, and Guevara's speeches describing it count only as his words.

sources.usedFor: Unequal exchange, socialist aid duty, state ownership and planning, foreign bases and debts, alliance with the socialist camp, arms free of charge, technological leap. Read in full.

sources.usedFor: The three lessons of the Cuban revolution, armed struggle and elections, the dictatorship of the reactionary classes, isolation of one country, worker and peasant base.

sources.title: Ernesto "Che" Guevara, intelectual latinoamericano: Notas para un estudio crítico de su pensamiento
sources.author: Hugo Cancino, Sociedades (Aalborg University)
sources.usedFor: Defining source: Guevarism as a current of the new left; its key texts (Notes 1960, Socialism and Man 1965, the Tricontinental); vanguard party, dictatorship of the proletariat, rejection of representative democracy, central planning, art.

sources.title: The spark that does not die
sources.author: Michael Löwy, International Viewpoint (1997)
sources.usedFor: Defining source: Guevarismo and the guevarist tradition; revolutionary humanism, against stagism, refusal of blind terrorism, planning against market fetishism, silence on socialist democracy.

sources.title: Economics Cannot be Separated from Politics (speech at the OAS conference, Punta del Este)
sources.author: Che Guevara (1961)
sources.usedFor: Democracy not only elections, nationalisations including banking, urban reform, abolition of racial discrimination, redistribution, free education, tax reform, workers' participation in management.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He held that revolution is won by armed struggle and would never disband the revolutionary army.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: At Punta del Este he praised Cuba's nationalisation of the banking system as an efficient instrument for exercising credit according to the country's needs, the opposite of leaving money to the market.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Nulled: the first pass answered from a general principle or a passage that fits either answer. Guevara's texts and the defining scholarship (Cancino, Löwy) state nothing that settles this statement.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about abolishing wage labour, not money, and the statement now asks only about money; wage labour has its own statement.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Nulled: the first pass answered from a general principle or a passage that fits either answer. Guevara's texts and the defining scholarship (Cancino, Löwy) state nothing that settles this statement.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: In 'Socialism and Man' he says people reach their full human condition when they are no longer compelled to sell themselves as a commodity, and wants work freed from that sale.

accelerate-technology.rationale: In Algiers he said poor countries must start from technology at its current level and make a great technological leap forward rather than climb slowly from feudalism.

alienated-labor.rationale: In 'Socialism and Man in Cuba' he describes capitalist labour as alienation and holds that socialism must free people from it.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: He told the Youth Congress the agrarian reform gave land to individual peasants who had worked small plots, alongside cooperatives, rather than making all land state property.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: He called for armed internationalism and 'two, three, many Vietnams', and personally led guerrillas in the Congo and Bolivia.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The foco doctrine holds that insurrection itself can create the subjective conditions for a broader uprising.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: The Tricontinental message praises the Vietnamese people's armed resistance to US forces and calls for creating many more such fronts.

arms-reduction.rationale: At the UN he backed general and complete disarmament and the destruction of all thermonuclear weapons, while refusing a regional denuclearisation pact as long as US bases remained.

central-bank-independence.rationale: He praised nationalising banking so credit serves the country's needs, and his budgetary system makes money and credit instruments of central planning, not of an independent bank.

central-planning.rationale: Guevara ran Cuban industry on the budgetary-finance system and rejected commodity relations, the law of value and material interest as levers of socialism.

character-from-environment.rationale: The New Man is created through education, daily action and new social foundations.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: At Punta del Este he presented Cuba's new childcare centres, workers' social centres and free education as achievements of the revolution, the opposite of cutting social provision.

decide-locally.rationale: His budgetary finance system rests on central control of each enterprise's plan and management by central bodies, and he credits centralisation with closing inefficient small workshops.

defeat-communism.rationale: He was a communist revolutionary who saw capitalism and imperialism as the enemy to be defeated, not coexisted with.

democracy-best.rationale: In 'Socialism and Man' he warns against transplanting bourgeois democracy and its legislative chambers into the new society, and Cancino reads him as rejecting representative democracy.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: At Punta del Este he endorsed the Cuban view that democracy cannot consist solely of elections, which are nearly always fictitious and managed by landowners and professional politicians.

direct-action.rationale: He held that power in Latin America is won mainly by armed struggle, calling it unpardonable to look only to elections, though he did not rule out gains through elections where they are possible.

notes: Second pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-09) under rules 5. Guevarism has no record (never a state's official doctrine), so every source is words. Answers rest on Guevara's own texts tied to the ideology by the defining sources (Cancino, Löwy) and the local Marxists Internet Archive corpus; Wikipedia only gave leads. First-pass answers deduced from a general value (socialism, materialism, egalitarianism) or from Cuban state practice were nulled with their history kept. Themes searched in the full texts: elections and parliaments, the party and the state, democracy, law and courts, executions, press and art, race, women, religion, health, education, land, banking, money, debt, trade and tariffs, foreign bases, disarmament, the UN and international law, sabotage and civilians. Guevara's published texts say nothing on gender, sexuality, family, religion policy, immigration or the environment, so those statements stay null. In 1961 at Punta del Este he guaranteed Cuba would not export revolution; his mature position (Algiers 1965, Tricontinental 1967) is armed internationalism, and the answers follow it.
